finding.claim: Authorization bypass on DELETE /files/<fid>: the handler calls the boolean predicate `is_allowed` (imported under the alias `require_allowed`) and discards the result. It never aborts, so the delete runs for any caller. The sibling rename handler correctly uses `ensure_allowed`, which calls abort(403).
finding.source: Any HTTP client, including an unauthenticated one with no grants, sends DELETE /files/<fid> with a known fid.
finding.sink: `del STORE[fid]` at views.py:19, which permanently deletes the file record.

trace.note: `is_allowed` is imported as `require_allowed`. The name suggests an enforcing check but it only returns a bool.
`is_allowed` returns True or False and never raises.
`f = STORE[fid]` loads the resource with no ownership scoping.
The return value of `require_allowed(...)` is discarded, so the check has no effect.

finding.guards_checked: The return value is not used. There is no abort or raise on a False result. No other auth middleware exists, since `before_request` only loads the user. The rename route uses `ensure_allowed` and is enforced (SAFE). The delete route has no enforced control.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: require_allowed (alias of boolean is_allowed, acl.py:4-5) is called at views.py:18 with result discarded; before_request (views.py:10-12) only loads user from a header
verdict.reason: views.py:4 aliases the boolean is_allowed as require_allowed, views.py:18 discards its result (acl.py:5 returns a bool and never aborts), so `del STORE[fid]` at views.py:19 runs for any caller, unlike the rename route's enforced ensure_allowed (views.py:26, acl.py:10).

finding.claim: Identity is taken directly from a client-supplied request header, `X-Session-User-Verified`, with no signature, session, or token verification in this code. Any client can impersonate any user who holds grants, for example by sending `X-Session-User-Verified: alice`. This is only safe if a trusted front proxy strips and sets the header. Nothing in this repo enforces that, so it is flagged as PLAUSIBLE.
finding.source: The `X-Session-User-Verified` HTTP request header, set by the client.
finding.sink: `ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "write")` at views.py:26 uses `g.user` for authorization, and rename writes `f["name"]` at views.py:27. The `is_allowed` call in delete at views.py:18 also uses `g.user`, but that result is discarded (see F1).

trace.note: `g.user = request.headers.get("X-Session-User-Verified")` is set straight from the header.
`ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "write")` trusts that value as the authenticated identity.
The grants lookup is keyed by the spoofed username string.
The file name is modified after the spoofed identity passes the ACL.

finding.guards_checked: No signature or HMAC check, no session lookup, and no header stripping in this repo. A trusted reverse proxy that strips and sets the header is outside the code I can see, so I could not confirm it. Resources with no grants for the user are denied, so exploitation needs knowledge of a username that has grants on the target file.

verdict.guard_found: none in repo. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 when the user has no grant, but it is keyed on the spoofable username. No header stripping or signature check exists.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 trusts the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header, and views.py:26 and acl.py:5 authorize on it, so any client could spoof it, but whether a front proxy strips and sets that header is outside this repo (only acl.py and views.py exist), so exploitability can't be decided.
